quote: The SSS from the Boston carpal tunnel syndrome questionnaire (BCTQ) [18] was used for primary outcome of symptoms at baseline and after 8 weeks of treatment.
proposed_wording: Randomised placebo-controlled trials of this cream with a pain endpoint in neuropathic or related pain states include Fassoulaki 2000 (the cream alone around breast-cancer surgery, preventing chronic post-mastectomy pain at three months), Fassoulaki 2005 (the cream inside a three-drug prevention package) and Strauss 2015 (complex regional pain syndrome type I, n=12, double-blind crossover with randomised session order, one application to the forearm rather than the painful hand; pain intensity did not change); none of them applied it to an established painful area as treatment. Two randomised placebo-cream-controlled trials in carpal tunnel syndrome also applied it to the forearm, to guide sensory relearning, and reported no separate pain measure: Flondell 2017 (n=70; primary endpoint the Boston symptom severity scale, a composite in which five of its eleven items concern pain; no difference from placebo) and Flondell 2024 (n=24; primary clinical outcome two-point discrimination; no difference from placebo in any clinical outcome).
reason: Answer to the question: the endpoint includes pain items, but pain is not reported separately from numbness. The symptom severity scale (Levine 1993, the paper's ref 18) is the mean of 11 items scored 1-5: items 1-5 are hand or wrist pain (severity at night, waking from pain at night, daytime pain, how often, how long an episode lasts) and items 6-11 are numbness, weakness, tingling, numbness or tingling at night, waking from it, and difficulty grasping small objects (item content as reproduced in Multanen 2020, PMID 32919457, and Leite 2006, PMID 17054773). Flondell 2017 reports only the total score (one mean per arm at baseline and 8 weeks, Table 2, PDF p. 5), with no item or pain/numbness breakdown and no pain VAS, NRS or other pain measure; 'pain' appears once, in the introduction. Trial facts: randomised (computer list), placebo cream visually and cosmetically identical, assessors blind (the researcher who applied the cream was not; patient blinding not stated), EMLA 34 and placebo 36 randomised, 32 and 36 analysed, 8-week follow-up and surgery status at 12 months; no between-group difference on the primary outcome (p = 0.78) or on QuickDASH, satisfaction VAS, monofilament, two-point discrimination or nerve conduction; the scale improved within the EMLA arm only (p = 0.001; a 0.5-unit change, below the 0.8 the authors take as clinically important). Judgement: a randomised placebo-controlled trial of this cream in an established compression neuropathy (the population element is met, consistent with A047 and E041 counting carpal tunnel syndrome as neuropathic pain), but its endpoint is a composite symptom score, not a neuropathic-pain endpoint, and the cream went on the forearm to guide sensory relearning, not on the painful area; it misses the outcome element, so it does not refute the uniqueness wording, and on this paper alone the claim stays narrowed, as it stood on Fassoulaki 2005. Note for the main session: a search this paper prompted found Strauss 2015 (PMID 26270587; see its extra-study entry), a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover of this cream on the forearm in chronic CRPS type I with pain intensity measured, which carries the claim to refuted if CRPS I is counted as neuropathic pain, as the D067 searches and the Reference do; under the strict-elements rule Fassoulaki 2005 (the cream inside a three-drug package) may also do so. The proposed wording above takes all of these in and corrects the description of both Flondell trials (Flondell 2024's primary clinical outcome was two-point discrimination; see its extra-study entry).

quote: EMLAV or placebo was applied to the volar aspect of the forearm, in an area from the wrist and 15 cm proximal on the same side as the CTS.
proposed_wording: Attal 1999 is the only study of repeated daily application combined with quantitative sensory testing in postherpetic neuralgia. Daily application has also been studied in painful carpal tunnel syndrome (Moghtaderi 2009, randomised, open-label, against steroid injection). Repeated non-daily application to the forearm rather than the symptomatic hand, to guide sensory relearning, has been studied after nerve repair (Rosén 2006 and Lundborg 2007, randomised, placebo-controlled, over two weeks), in vibration-induced neuropathy (Rosén 2011, case series, up to a year or more) and in carpal tunnel syndrome (Flondell 2017, randomised, placebo-cream-controlled, over eight weeks); none of these reports a separate pain measure. Outside neuropathic pain, daily application has been studied in chronic leg-ulcer pain over ten days (Effendy 2015, open and uncontrolled, no patient described as neuropathic) and for four weeks as a wound dressing (Purcell 2017, pilot randomised trial).
reason: Flondell element only (D066's own question is answered from Effendy 2015 by S-686-07; the last sentence of the wording is that entry's, kept so the two merge). What the study did: the cream went on the volar forearm on the side of the carpal tunnel syndrome, from the wrist proximally, not on the hand, for 90 minutes each time, three times in week 1, twice a week in weeks 2-6 and once a week in weeks 7-8 (15 applications over 8 weeks), with sensory re-education; the aim was forearm deafferentation to guide cortical plasticity, not analgesia (PDF pp. 2-3). So it is a dataset of repeated, non-daily application in an established compression neuropathy, but not of daily application, not on the symptomatic skin, and in patients neither selected for pain nor assessed for pain separately (a composite symptom score in which five of eleven items concern pain, plus sensory tests). It is therefore not repeated daily application in an established neuropathic pain state in D066's sense, and adds nothing to the refutation, which rests on Moghtaderi 2009 and is unchanged. The current reason's listing of Flondell 2017 among 'repeated-application datasets in established neuropathies' is accurate only as non-daily forearm application; Lundborg 2007 and Rosén 2006 (the paper's refs 17 and 10, apparently one nerve-repair trial) are early reinnervation after repair, not an established pain state.

Two randomised placebo-cream-controlled trials in carpal tunnel syndrome also applied it to the forearm, to guide sensory relearning, and reported no separate pain measure: Flondell 2017 (n=70; primary endpoint the Boston symptom severity scale, a composite in which five of its eleven items concern pain; no difference from placebo) and Flondell 2024 (n=24; primary clinical outcome two-point discrimination; no difference from placebo in any clinical outcome).
reason: Led to it by S-686-43: the same group's later trial, named in D067's current proposed wording (it postdates Flondell 2017, so it is not in that paper's reference list). Full text (PMC11563718): a separate cohort (24 patients with unilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, its own ethics approval), the same forearm regimen with daily sensory training in both arms, randomised from a computer list (one patient received placebo instead of EMLA, giving 11 and 13); the primary clinical outcome was within-group change in two-point discrimination, with dexterity, the symptom severity scale and QuickDASH secondary, plus fMRI of the somatosensory cortex; no between-group difference in any clinical outcome; the symptom severity scale improved within the placebo arm only; no pain measure. On its own it is a further randomised placebo-controlled trial of this cream in an established compression neuropathy without a neuropathic-pain endpoint, so it narrows at most and the standing verdict narrowed is kept. It corrects the current proposed wording, which says both Flondell trials used composite symptom-severity endpoints and were negative on their primary outcome: in the 2024 trial the primary clinical outcome was two-point discrimination, which improved within the EMLA arm, while every between-group comparison was non-significant.

quote: In a double-blinded placebo-controlled study, we enrolled 12 patients with unilateral CRPS I of the hand in the chronic state. … Pain intensity was not modulated after intervention.
proposed_wording: Randomised placebo-controlled trials of this cream with a pain endpoint in neuropathic or related pain states include Fassoulaki 2000 (the cream alone around breast-cancer surgery, preventing chronic post-mastectomy pain at three months), Fassoulaki 2005 (the cream inside a three-drug prevention package) and Strauss 2015 (complex regional pain syndrome type I, n=12, double-blind crossover with randomised session order, one application to the forearm rather than the painful hand; pain intensity did not change); none of them applied it to an established painful area as treatment. Two randomised placebo-cream-controlled trials in carpal tunnel syndrome also applied it to the forearm, to guide sensory relearning, and reported no separate pain measure: Flondell 2017 (n=70; primary endpoint the Boston symptom severity scale, a composite in which five of its eleven items concern pain; no difference from placebo) and Flondell 2024 (n=24; primary clinical outcome two-point discrimination; no difference from placebo in any clinical outcome).
reason: Led to it by S-686-43: found by a PubMed search for forearm-anaesthesia (guided-plasticity) trials that this paper prompted; it is not in Flondell 2017's reference list. The abstract never names the cream, so the D067 searches (EMLA and lidocaine-prilocaine terms) could not retrieve it. The full paper, reprinted in the first author's Greifswald dissertation (free at the German National Library, d-nb.info/113254338X/34), names it as EMLA against an aqueous placebo cream, applied once per session to the volar forearm of the affected side in a double-blind crossover whose session order was randomised (the authors call the design pseudorandomised; 6 of 12 had placebo first), with pain intensity rated on a 10 cm VAS at rest before and after each session and not altered; the primary aims were tactile acuity and intracortical inhibition. It matches every element of D067 as the record scopes neuropathic pain (the D067 searches included 'complex regional', and the Reference counts CRPS trials in its neuropathic-pain evidence), and it is a treatment-setting trial, so it contradicts both 'the only randomised placebo-controlled trial with a neuropathic-pain endpoint' and 'it is prevention rather than treatment'. Uncertain because CRPS type I has no demonstrable nerve lesion and so does not meet the IASP definition of neuropathic pain, because pain was a secondary measure after a single application to skin outside the painful area, and because the allocation is described as pseudorandomised; if the main session excludes CRPS I, this source narrows rather than refutes.
